cases.summary: A transcript exactly as puller/pull_sessions.py writes it, LF line endings.
covers: role from the first line of a block

cases.summary: The same transcript with CRLF line endings (what a text-mode writer produces on Windows; the puller wrote such files before commit 34e84d3).
cases.difference: Apple splits on LF only and its inline trim does not remove CR: no separator is recognised, all turns merge into one message, the title and the source URL end in a carriage return, and the code block never closes. The web app normalises line endings first and must return exactly the result of the LF fixture.

cases.summary: The same transcript with a UTF-8 byte-order mark in front.
What the puller writes when it harvested no turns: the two header lines and nothing else.
cases.difference: Apple saves a session with zero messages and reports success. The web app must not save it.

cases.summary: Two sessions in one file, as written by the puller's --combine option (files joined by a blank line).
cases.difference: Apple reads the file as one session: the second header and its first turn become a single message of role unknown. The web app starts a new session at every header pair that begins a block.

cases.summary: Puller-shaped markdown whose Source line is not a claude.ai link.
cases.difference: Apple knows one host only (claude.ai) and labels everything else Other. The web app maps the link host to a provider.

cases.summary: A ChatGPT data export (conversations.json) with three conversations.
covers: unknown author role kept as role unknown
parts joined with a newline and trimmed

cases.summary: A single conversation object (not wrapped in an array) with a mapping; the file starts with a UTF-8 byte-order mark.
covers: byte-order mark in front of JSON (JSON.parse rejects it unless it is removed)

cases.summary: An export array in which one entry has no mapping.
cases.difference: Apple rejects the whole array as a ChatGPT export and then imports the raw JSON text as one Note. The web app imports the valid conversations and skips the others.

cases.summary: A malformed export in which two nodes name each other as parent.
cases.difference: Apple follows `parent` links with no cycle check: the importer never returns and its node list grows without bound (confirmed with a watchdog: no result after 400 ms, while the same data without the cycle returns in about 20 ms). The web app stops at the first node it has already visited.

cases.summary: A conversation with no current_node and no message timestamps.
cases.difference: Without current_node Apple sorts the mapping's values by message create_time. The values come from a dictionary with no defined order and the sort is not stable, so messages with equal or missing times come out in a different order on every run. The web app uses a stable sort and keeps the order of the keys in the JSON text for ties.

cases.summary: A .json file that is not a ChatGPT export. Stand-in for the puller's <id>.json payload, whose real schema is not documented in the repository.
cases.difference: Apple imports the raw JSON text as one message of role unknown and labels it Claude because the text contains that word. The web app refuses it with a clear reason and lets the user choose to keep it as a plain-text note.

cases.summary: Plain text with every kind of speaker marker, LF line endings.
covers: Name: markers with text on the same line

cases.summary: The same text with CRLF line endings (a file saved by Windows Notepad).
cases.difference: Apple misses every marker that has no colon (the line ends in a carriage return), leaves CR characters inside the stored text, and the code block never closes when the message is displayed. The web app must return exactly the result of the LF fixture.

cases.summary: Plain notes with no speaker markers at all.
A note that names assistants, each on its own line, but is not a dialogue.
cases.difference: Apple treats the three name lines as speaker markers (the last paragraph becomes an assistant message) and labels the session Claude because the word occurs in the text. The web app ignores bare names unless the text has both a user and an assistant marker, and never guesses the provider from words in the content.

cases.summary: A file that contains only spaces, a tab and newlines.
cases.difference: Apple saves a session that holds one empty message. The web app rejects the file as empty.

cases.summary: A zero-byte file.
Fenced code blocks in every shape the display splitter handles: language, no language, indented fence, empty block, unterminated block.
A code block whose lines look like speaker markers.
cases.difference: Apple splits the assistant's message at `user:`, `system:` and `ai:` inside the code block, producing five messages and a broken block. The web app does not look for markers inside a closed fenced block.

cases.summary: Bold text on the same line as a speaker marker.
cases.difference: Apple deletes every `**` on a marker line, so bold markup after the label is lost. The web app removes `**` only where it decorates the label itself.

cases.summary: One assistant turn of more than 3,000 characters between two short turns.

Accented Latin (composed and decomposed), Japanese, Arabic, Cyrillic, emoji including a joined family sequence, a marker preceded by a no-break space, a full-width colon, and two lines that end in a zero width space followed by a line holding only U+0085.
covers: no Unicode normalisation of stored text
full-width colon is not a marker
exact trim sets: U+200B and U+0085 are removed at the ends, which JavaScript trim() does not do

cases.summary: UTF-16 little-endian text with a byte-order mark and CRLF (what Windows PowerShell 5 writes with `>`).
cases.difference: Apple decodes files as UTF-8 only; this file yields no session and the message 'No sessions found in the selected files.' The web app detects the byte-order mark, decodes UTF-16 and imports the transcript, flagging the encoding it used.

cases.summary: Windows-1252 (ANSI) text with an accented letter, an en dash and curly quotes.
cases.difference: Not valid UTF-8, so Apple imports nothing. The web app falls back to windows-1252 for text that is not UTF-8 and flags it.

cases.summary: The visible text of a claude.ai share page (synthetic), pasted.
covers: text before the first header dropped

cases.summary: The same share-page text with CRLF line endings.
cases.difference: With CR left at the end of every line Apple no longer recognises the exact-match furniture (Copy, Retry), blank lines or the '10:42 AM' time lines, and keeps CR characters in the text. The web app must return exactly the result of the LF fixture.

cases.summary: Share-page text whose answer contains indented code, repeated lines, and lines that look like page furniture.
cases.difference: Apple trims every line (indentation is lost) and drops any line equal to the previous non-empty one (a repeated statement disappears). The web app keeps indentation and never removes an indented line. Still removed in both, by design of the heuristic: the second unindented `print` line, the line `Share` and the line `10:30`.

cases.summary: Page text with 'You said:' and 'ChatGPT said:' headers (synthetic).
covers: share-page parser fires on any 'You said:'
cases.difference: Apple's share parser knows only 'You said:' and 'Claude responded:'. Every answer is appended to the question before it, all messages are user messages, and the session is labelled Claude. The web app also accepts 'ChatGPT said:', 'Gemini said:' and 'Claude said:' as assistant headers and takes the provider from the header family.

cases.summary: Share-page text in which two turns have text only on their header line.
cases.difference: Apple discards the text after 'You said:' as a preview. A turn with nothing else vanishes: here both user turns are lost. The web app falls back to the header-line text when a turn has no body.

cases.summary: The clipboard holds a single link.
cases.note: Nothing is imported. The Apple app opens its capture browser at `link_url`; the web app shows the link help of capture.md section 8.1 (and offers server capture where that tier exists).

cases.summary: The clipboard holds one word that ends in a full stop.
cases.difference: Apple treats any single token under 500 characters that contains a dot as a link and opens the capture browser at https://Thanks. The web app uses `looksLikeLink` of capture.md section 8.1 (the host must contain a dot, must not end in a dot, and must end in a label of two or more letters); this text is not a link and is imported as a note.

cases.summary: The clipboard holds only white space.
A short dialogue surrounded and interleaved with blank lines, spaces and tabs; the provider picker is set to Gemini.
Puller markdown pasted with two blank lines in front of the header.
cases.difference: Apple requires the header on the very first line. Here detection fails, the generic parser takes over, the header becomes a Note, every message keeps a trailing '---', and the title is 'Pasted session'. The web app skips leading blank lines.

cases.summary: The text of a signed-out landing page, pasted.
covers: sign-in wall guard on pasted text
cases.difference: In the Apple app the sign-in-wall guard exists only on the capture path: pasted wall text is saved as a session. The web app applies the same test to pasted text and answers `sign_in_suspected`; the user may then choose to import anyway.

cases.summary: Pasted page text together with the link it was copied from (the link field of capture.md section 8.1).
cases.difference: The Apple paste path has no link: the session gets the picker's provider and an empty source URL. In the web app the link becomes the source URL and its host decides the provider, whatever the picker says.

cases.summary: A context pack, the Apple app's own export (ContextPack.swift), pasted back in. One message contains a '---' line of its own.
cases.difference: Apple has no parser for its own export: the header block becomes a Note, every message keeps a trailing '---', the '**Note:**' turn is glued to the previous message, and title, link, tags and summary are lost. OPTIONAL for the web app (data-model.md prefers the interchange format for transfers): a parser that reads the format back into title, provider, model, link, tags, summary and clean messages.

cases.summary: Four harvested turn blocks from a claude.ai page, with a title detected on the page.
Two harvested turn blocks from a chatgpt.com link, no title detected and none typed.
covers: title falls back to the last path component
cases.difference: Apple labels every multi-turn capture that is not from claude.ai as Other. The web app maps the link host to a provider.

cases.summary: The first turn (more than 700 characters) starts with page-header lines; the last turn is a page footer.
covers: page-header residue stripped from the first turn

cases.summary: The same shape with a short first turn (under 700 characters).
covers: chrome test runs before header stripping
cases.difference: Apple tests the raw first turn for chrome before it strips header lines. A turn under 700 characters that contains 'sign in' is dropped whole, so the user's question is lost. The web app strips the header lines first and judges what is left.

cases.summary: A conversation whose first and last turns are short and happen to contain the letters 'sign in'.
cases.note: Both real turns are classified as chrome and dropped, in the Apple app and by the same test in the web app. This weakness of the heuristic is kept on purpose (see import-rules.md, defect D4). What must change is outside this result: the Apple app drops silently, the web app must show `dropped_turns` to the user and let them be restored before saving.

cases.summary: The whole-page text of a signed-out landing page.
cases.note: The guard function must give the same answer. In the Apple app nothing is saved and a one-line status asks the user to log in and capture again. The web app reports `sign_in_suspected` as a warning and must also offer 'import anyway' (allow_wall).

cases.summary: A whole-page capture of a short, real conversation that mentions 'sign in' and 'log in'.
cases.note: A false positive of the guard: under 1,200 characters with two marker phrases. The function result is kept identical. The Apple app gives the user no way to save this conversation; the web app must offer 'import anyway' (next fixture).

cases.summary: The same capture again, after the user answered the warning with 'import anyway' (allow_wall is true).
cases.difference: The Apple app has no override: the capture stays refused. In the web app the guard only warns; with allow_wall the capture is imported normally.

cases.summary: A whole-page capture (one block) of a claude.ai share page; the user typed a name.
covers: single-block capture runs the text parsers
typed name wins over the detected title

cases.summary: A whole-page capture from a Gemini link: no speaker labels at all, the first line is the word 'Gemini', and the conversation mentions Claude.
cases.difference: This reproduces how a whole page becomes one mislabelled message. Apple: the first line is a bare-name marker, so the whole page becomes ONE message of role assistant, and the keyword scan finds 'claude' before 'gemini', so the session is labelled Claude although the link is a Gemini link. The web app takes the provider from the link host, does not honour a lone bare name, and keeps the page as one message of role unknown for the user to review. Nothing in this text allows a split.

cases.summary: The same conversation with the label lines 'You said' and 'Gemini said' (no colon) that an earlier review reported for Gemini chat pages. Unverified against a live page.
covers: Gemini label lines without a colon
cases.difference: Apple knows these labels only with a colon, so the result is the same single assistant message labelled Claude. The web app accepts the two whole-line labels when BOTH occur in the text and splits the page into turns. The rule is built on a reported page layout, not on an observed one; if real pages differ it simply does not fire and the previous fixture applies.

cases.summary: Every harvested block is page chrome.
The capture returned no text at all.
Two of the four blocks consist of a speaker label and nothing else.
cases.difference: Apple stores a message with empty text for each label-only block. The web app never stores an empty message.

cases.summary: A harvested turn that contains indented code with a repeated line.
covers: furniture cleaning damages code in captured turns
cases.difference: Every captured turn goes through the share-page cleaner. Apple flattens the indentation and deletes the repeated call. The web app keeps indented lines exactly.

cases.summary: A harvested turn with a fenced code block whose lines look like page furniture (capture.md fences code at extraction time).
cases.difference: Apple applies the furniture rules inside the fence too: the lines `Copy`, `10:30` and `Share`, the repeated `make build` and one of the two blank lines disappear from the code. The web app copies a closed fenced block untouched; the `Copy` line after the block is still removed.

cases.summary: Unit cases for looksLikeSignInWall: both length thresholds, both hit thresholds, how markers are counted, and that length is counted in user-perceived characters.
Unit cases for stripChromeTurns: the 700-character limit, each chrome condition, the header-line rules (90 characters, 12 lines), and the order of the two steps.
cases.difference: Only the two cases whose name starts with ORDER differ. Apple judges the raw first turn, so header residue condemns the whole turn. The web app strips header lines first. The second ORDER case shows the price: a page name that used to be dropped with its 'Sign in' line now survives as a short turn.

cases.summary: Unit cases for the display splitter that turns one message text into prose and code blocks.
cases.difference: Only the four cases whose name starts with DIFFERENT differ. Apple: CR breaks every fence; a line that starts with three backticks always opens a block, even when it is a one-line code span; fences are exactly three backticks, so a four-backtick fence is mis-split. The web app normalises line endings and follows the CommonMark fence rules for backtick fences.

cases.summary: Text in the share-page shape as a person types it: a sentence on each speaker line, a blank line, more text.
covers: text on a speaker line is the first line of the turn
the blank line after it is kept
cases.difference: Apple discards the text after 'You said:' and 'Claude responded:' whenever more text follows: the first sentence of both turns is lost. The web app keeps it as the first line of the turn, because the line after it does not begin with it.

cases.summary: Share-page text whose speaker lines end in an ellipsis like a preview, while the text after them does not repeat it.
covers: a preview that the next line does not begin with is kept
the ellipsis is cut for the comparison only
cases.difference: Apple discards the text after the header as a preview. Here the next line does not begin with it, so the words exist nowhere else and are lost. The web app drops such text only when the first non-blank line after it begins with it, after one trailing ellipsis has been cut for the comparison; otherwise it keeps the text as the first line of the turn, ellipsis included.

cases.summary: Share-page text whose speaker lines hold one short word that the next line begins a longer word with: 'No' before 'Nothing', 'Yes' before 'Yesterday'.
covers: without an ellipsis, text on a speaker line is a preview only if it ends where a word ends
a short first line that begins the next line's first word is kept
cases.difference: Apple discards the text after the header whenever more text follows: 'No' and 'Yes' are lost. The web app takes such text for a preview only when the next line begins with it and, no ellipsis having been cut, the text ends where a word ends. 'Nothing' continues 'No' with a letter, so 'No' is kept as the first line of the turn.

cases.summary: Share-page text whose speaker-line text is followed in the next line by a digit ('Version 1' before 'Version 10') and by a combining mark ('Cafe' before 'Cafe' with U+0301).
covers: a digit after the repeated text means it is not a preview
a combining mark after the repeated text means it is not a preview
cases.difference: Apple discards the text after the header whenever more text follows. The web app keeps it here: the next line begins with it, but continues with a digit in one turn and with a combining mark in the other, so the text does not end where a word ends and is the first line of the turn.

cases.summary: Share-page text in which a code fence opens on the speaker line itself and closes two lines later, in both turns. The line between the fences is a word that pages print as a button label: 'Report', 'Retry'.
covers: a fenced block that opens on a speaker line protects the lines inside it
the text of a speaker line is not taken for a preview of its own closing fence
cases.difference: Apple discards the text after the header whenever more text follows, and removes a label line also inside a fenced block: each turn is left with its closing fence alone, and 'Report' and 'Retry' are stored nowhere. The web app reads the lines of a turn twice, alone and with the text of the speaker line in front, and never removes a line that either reading puts inside a closed fenced block. Read alone, the turn begins with a line that is no preview target for the fence, so the fence stays the first line of its turn and the block is kept whole.

cases.summary: Share-page text with a fence on both speaker lines. In the first turn the fence is a preview: the turn repeats it and then closes the block. In the second turn a time line stands between the speaker line and the next fence, so each of the two readings of the turn closes a different block.
covers: a fence on a speaker line that the turn repeats is a preview and is dropped once
a line inside a closed block under either reading of the turn is kept
the text of a speaker line is kept when the first line of the turn does not begin with it
cases.difference: Apple leaves each turn with one fence line: 'Report', '10:42' and 'Retry' are stored nowhere. In the first turn the web app finds the fence of the speaker line again as the first line of the turn, takes it for a preview and drops it once; the block that the turn closes by itself keeps 'Report'. In the second turn the two readings close different blocks: with the speaker line in front, the time line is inside a block; read alone, 'Retry' is. Both lines are kept, the first line of the turn does not begin with the fence, and so the text of the speaker line stays the first line of the turn.

cases.summary: Share-page text in which a user turn holds a closed code block that quotes two speaker lines of an older conversation.
covers: a line that begins with a speaker label inside a closed fenced block is text, not a header
the block stays whole in its turn
cases.difference: Apple has no fence rule in the share-page parser and removes the text on a speaker line: the two quoted lines become turns of their own, and what is left of the conversation is two fence lines. Until 2026-11-20 the web rule also began a turn at every line that begins with a speaker label. Now such a line is text when it stands inside a closed fenced block and the fences of the paste pair up: the block stays whole in the user turn, and the label words are stored with it.

cases.summary: A transcript with generic markers ('**Human:**', '**Assistant:**') whose first message quotes two share-page speaker lines inside a closed code block.
covers: speaker lines that stand only inside a closed block do not make a text share-page text
the generic parser reads the text, and nothing above the quoted lines is lost
cases.difference: Apple takes the text for share-page text because one line begins with 'You said:', and stores one assistant message that starts at the closing fence: the first message and both quoted lines are stored nowhere. In the web app the two speaker lines are text, because they stand inside a closed block; no header is left, so this is not share-page text, and the generic parser reads it: two messages, nothing lost.

cases.summary: A plain note of three lines; the second begins with 'Claude responded:'. No line begins with a user label.
covers: text with speaker lines of one kind only is not share-page text
the line above the speaker line is kept
cases.difference: Apple takes the note for share-page text, drops the line above the speaker line and the text on it, and stores 'More notes.' as an assistant message. The web app asks for a user header and an assistant header before it reads text as a share page. Here there is no user header, so the generic parser reads the text: the first line is kept as a note, and 'Claude responded:' is a marker of that parser.

cases.summary: Share-page text whose first turn opens a code block that never closes; later turns follow, one of them with a closed block. The fences of the text do not pair up.
covers: when the fences of a text do not pair up, no speaker line is taken for text
cases.difference: Apple removes the text on the speaker lines and keeps two user messages. In the web app the first block never closes, so the fences of the paste do not pair up. No reading of them can be trusted then, and every line that begins with a speaker label stays a header: four turns, as written. Without this guard the lone fence would pair with the opening fence of the later block and hide two speaker lines.

cases.summary: One line of ordinary text above a two-line dialogue in the share-page shape. The line is not page furniture. The Apple app keeps the line too, for a reason of its own: it discards the text on both speaker lines, finds no turn, and reads the paste with its generic parser.
covers: text above the first speaker line is kept as a note unless it is the top of a share page

cases.summary: Five lines above a two-turn dialogue in the share-page shape: a line of text, an indented line 'Report', and a closed code block that holds the words 'log in'.
covers: above the first speaker line, only a line that the cleaner could remove counts as page furniture
an indented line and a line inside a closed fenced block are text, whatever words they hold
cases.difference: Apple drops what stands above the first speaker line, whatever it is. The web app drops such lines only when they are the top of a share page, and it looks for page furniture only among the lines that its cleaner could remove. 'Report' is indented and 'log in' stands inside a closed code block, so neither is a sign of a page top: the five lines are kept as a note.

cases.summary: A page top of two lines above a two-turn dialogue: 'Shared conversation', and a line of 678 ASCII characters and one emoji. Joined by a line break they have 699 user-perceived characters and 700 UTF-16 units. The web app drops them as the top of a share page, as the Apple app drops everything above the first speaker line. A port that compares `length` with 700 keeps them as a note and fails here.
covers: the 700 of the page-top test is counted in user-perceived characters

cases.summary: The same shape with a second line of 680 ASCII characters: the two lines above the first speaker line have 700 characters.
covers: lines above the first speaker line with 700 characters or more are not the top of a share page
they are kept as a note, the line with the furniture phrase included
cases.difference: Apple drops what stands above the first speaker line. In the web app 700 characters are not fewer than 700, so the two lines are not the top of a share page, although one of them holds a furniture phrase: both are kept as a note.
